title: Soap, Then Baking Powder, Then Gum: Wrigley's First Year in Chicago
conflicts: Starting money: Wrigley (1922) says $32 and his experience; EWB and EBSCO add a $5,000 loan from an uncle (William Scotchard) with a cousin as partner; both given, the loan attributed. Gum maker: Zeno with a 1909 buyout (IDCH) vs 'Zero' and 1911 (EBSCO, EWB); story says 'an outside firm'. Juicy Fruit/Spearmint dated 1893 (IDCH, Penn State) or 1893/1894 (EWB, EBSCO); no date given. 1907 advertising spend ranges from $250,000-$284,000 (reference works) to $3 million (Wrigley himself); left out of the story.
notes: Anchored on Wrigley's first-person 1922 Illustrated World interview (S. J. Duncan Clark), cited from a todayinsci.com transcription with volume and pages. The other sources are reference works (IDCH, EWB, EBSCO Research Starters) and Penn State's Pennsylvania Center for the Book; no newspaper source loads (NYT and Britannica are blocked). 'Everybody likes something extra, for nothing' is unsourced in EWB, so it is paraphrased. Quote stance is 'complicates' (obstinacy vs caprice).
